research_notes:
MCD 10-K FY2025: revenue $26,885M; franchised revenues $16,548M; company-operated sales $9,690M; franchised margins $13,930M vs company-operated margins $1,422M; operating income $12,393M, margin 46.1%; 45,356 restaurants ~95% franchised; owns ~56% of land and ~80% of buildings (consolidated markets); rent and royalties based on % of sales; 20-year terms. Rents $10.4B / royalties $6.0B / fees $0.1B (FourWeekMBA citing 10-K; sums to the 10-K total).
Erlinger open letter 29 May 2024: Big Mac avg $4.39 (2019) -> $5.29 (+21%); $18 meal at 1 of 13,700+ locations; franchisees own >95% US restaurants and set prices to cover supply chain, wage and inflation costs. CNBC/NBC paraphrase: average menu item up ~40% since 2019.
History: 1940 San Bernardino; 1948 Speedee, 15c hamburger; 1954 Kroc (mixer salesman); 15 Apr 1955 Des Plaines; 1961 buyout $2.7M (McDonald's history). Handshake 1% royalty claim only from a nephew (Wikipedia Ray Kroc).
Sonneborn: ex-Tastee-Freez finance VP; Franchise Realty 1957; land on 10-year contract for deed, bank loan for building, lease at 40% markup + 5% of sales above base; Kroc autobiography 'beginning of real income'; >100 restaurants 1959, ~200 Aug 1960; 1961 $1.5M loan from three insurers for 22.5% equity (Restaurant Finance). 'Real estate business' line is from The Founder (2016). First president 1959, resigned 8 Jun 1967 over expansion vs recession (Wikipedia).
FDD (Franchise Chatter Oct 2026): fee $45,000; investment $1,472,000-$2,807,000; royalty 4-5%; advertising >=4%; effective rent 0-33.37% (2025); avg franchised US sales $4,057,000; operating income before occupancy $864K at $3.4M (25.4%).
Royalty 4% -> 5% for new US/Canada restaurants from 1 Jan 2024; ~$36,000/yr on $3.6M (The Takeout).
NOA survey (>100 franchisees, via Restaurant Business, Sept 2026): 95% profit fell Q1 2026; 97% plan not improving cash flow; ~8 in 10 cash flow can't cover reinvestment; 99% higher food/paper costs; remodel cycle 2027-28 $400K-$700K per store; Kempczinski 'They've got a lot of borrowing capacity still.'
July 29 2024: global comps -1%, first since pandemic; Kempczinski quote on price increases (NRN). Sept 2 2025: Extra Value Meals ~15% off; lower-income visits down double digits industrywide Q2; 'That absolutely is shaping value perceptions in a negative way.' (Fortune).

plan.title: Why McDonald's Got So Expensive (Follow the Rent)
alt_titles: McDonald's Is a Landlord That Sells Burgers
How McDonald's Really Makes Money (It's Not Burgers)
plan.description:
McDonald's collected $10.4 billion in rent in 2025, more than it made from royalties. This is how McDonald's really makes money as a landlord, why menu prices rose about 40% since 2019, and why I think the rent model explains who pays when prices go up.

How McDonald's makes money: from Harry Sonneborn's 1957 Franchise Realty idea to a company with a 46% operating margin, plus what franchise owners and customers say about the squeeze.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:45 The milkshake salesman
1:50 The landlord
4:00 The money machine
5:40 The franchisee's side
7:30 The customer pays
8:50 The verdict

segments.narration: Every time you buy a Big Mac, part of what you pay ends up as rent.
Last year, McDonald's collected ten point four billion dollars of it.
Not from selling burgers. From renting buildings to the people who sell the burgers.
Meanwhile, the price of a Big Mac in the US went from about four thirty-nine in 2019 to five twenty-nine by 2024. That's McDonald's own number.
Across the menu, the average item cost around forty percent more than in 2019.
So customers got angry. Franchise owners say they're barely making it. And the company makes more profit than ever from a percentage of every sale.
Which raises a question. Who actually made McDonald's so expensive?
I think the answer is hiding in the rent. To see why, we have to go back to 1957, and a finance man most people have never heard of.
First, the burgers. In 1940, two brothers, Dick and Mac McDonald, opened a drive-in in San Bernardino, California.
In 1948, they cut the menu right down and built a fast, self-service kitchen around a fifteen-cent hamburger. They called it the Speedee Service System.
In 1954, a milkshake-machine salesman called Ray Kroc came to see why this one restaurant was buying so many of his mixers.
He became their franchise agent, and on April fifteenth, 1955, he opened his own McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois.
The idea was simple. Kroc would sell the McDonald's system to other owners across the country, and take a small cut of their sales.
But selling franchises for a small cut of burger sales was hard money. The franchisees were thriving. McDonald's itself was not.
Then a former finance executive from Tastee-Freez, Harry Sonneborn, came up with a different idea.
Don't just sell franchises. Own the ground they stand on.
In 1957, they set up a company called Franchise Realty. Here's how it worked.
The company would find a site and buy the land on a ten-year contract. A bank loan paid for the building.
Then it leased the whole thing to the franchisee, at a forty percent markup over its own payments.
And on top of that, once sales passed a set level, the franchisee paid rent of five percent of sales.
And if a franchisee already owned the land? The company leased it from them, and then leased it straight back to them.
Think about what that does. McDonald's is now paid twice. Once for the brand, and once for the building.
And if a franchisee fails, the company still owns the land.
Ray Kroc later wrote in his autobiography that this was the beginning of real income for McDonald's.

visual.text: This was the beginning of *real income* for McDonald's.

segments.narration: You might know the famous line, you're not in the burger business, you're in the real estate business.

visual.text: You're not in the burger business, you're in the *real estate* business.

segments.narration: To be accurate, that exact sentence comes from the 2016 film The Founder. But the idea was real. Sonneborn sold bankers on McDonald's as a property business.
And bankers listened. By 1959, more than a hundred restaurants were open. By August 1960, close to two hundred.
In 1960 came its first loan from an institution: a two hundred and sixty thousand dollar mortgage at six percent, which paid for six restaurants. Lenders liked the land underneath.
In 1961, three insurance companies lent one and a half million dollars, and took twenty-two and a half percent of the company's equity in return.
That same year, Kroc bought out the McDonald brothers for two point seven million dollars.
Kroc wanted to pay it in installments. The brothers said no. They wanted the full amount.
A family member later claimed Kroc also promised them a one percent royalty on a handshake. There's no written proof it existed, and it was never paid.
The brothers also kept their original restaurant. Kroc was furious, and opened a new McDonald's nearby. The original, renamed the Big M, eventually closed.
And Sonneborn? He ran the company as its first president, until 1967.
He believed a recession was coming and wanted to stop building. Kroc wanted to keep expanding. Sonneborn resigned, and Kroc took his title.
But his machine stayed. And today, it's enormous.
At the end of 2025, there were forty-five thousand three hundred and fifty-six McDonald's restaurants. About ninety-five percent are run by franchisees.
In the markets it runs directly, McDonald's owns about fifty-six percent of the land under its restaurants, and about eighty percent of the buildings.
Total revenue in 2025 was about twenty-six point nine billion dollars.
Just under ten billion came from restaurants McDonald's runs itself. Sixteen and a half billion came from franchisees.
And look at what that franchise money is made of. Royalties, about six billion. Rent, about ten point four billion.
So McDonald's makes more from being a landlord than from its own brand fees.
And these deals are long. Franchise agreements generally run for twenty years.
Now the profit. The restaurants McDonald's runs itself made about one point four billion dollars in margin.
The franchised side made thirteen point nine billion. About ten times as much.
That's why McDonald's operating margin was forty-six percent. For a restaurant company, that's extraordinary.
Here's the key detail. Both rent and royalties are tied to a percentage of sales.
So when menu prices go up, sales go up. And McDonald's collects more, without paying the higher wages or food costs itself.
Who does pay those costs? The franchisee. So let's look at the deal from their side of the counter.
Buying into McDonald's in the US starts with a forty-five thousand dollar franchise fee.
The total start-up cost runs from about one point five to two point eight million dollars.
Then, every year, a royalty of four or five percent of sales. At least four percent more for advertising. And rent.
In 2025, the effective rent across franchised restaurants ranged from nothing at all up to thirty-three percent of sales.
To put that in dollars: at twenty percent rent, a restaurant doing four million a year in sales would pay eight hundred thousand dollars a year to its landlord. And the landlord is often McDonald's.
And in January 2024, McDonald's raised the royalty on new US restaurants from four to five percent.
Existing owners kept the old rate. The new one hits restaurants that are newly built, or bought straight from the company.
On a typical restaurant doing three point six million in sales, that extra point is about thirty-six thousand dollars a year.
A franchised US restaurant open at least a year averaged about four million dollars in sales in 2025.
Sounds great. But McDonald's own disclosure shows operating income before rent and fees at roughly a quarter of sales. Rent, royalties and loan payments all come out of that.

visual.label:
left before rent,
fees and debt

segments.narration: To be fair, McDonald's says about two thirds of its franchisees beat the eight hundred and sixty-four thousand dollar benchmark in that disclosure. Plenty of owners do well.
And the people running them say that number is shrinking.
In 2026, an independent franchisee group, the National Owners Association, surveyed more than a hundred owners. Restaurant Business reported the results.
Ninety-five percent said their restaurant-level profit fell in the first quarter of 2026. Ninety-nine percent said food and paper costs had gone up.

shots.label: hit by higher food and paper costs

segments.narration: Ninety-seven percent said the company's current plan isn't improving their cash flow.

visual.label: say the plan isn't helping cash flow

segments.narration: Nearly eight in ten said their cash flow can't cover the reinvestment McDonald's requires.
And here's the strangest number. All but three percent said their control over pricing had been weakened, or taken away.

visual.label:
say their pricing control
was weakened or removed

segments.narration: Remember that, because it's about to matter.
And that reinvestment is coming. Owners expect a new remodel cycle starting around 2027 to cost four hundred to seven hundred thousand dollars per restaurant. Paid by them.
Asked about it, McDonald's chief executive Chris Kempczinski said franchisees still have a lot of borrowing capacity.

visual.text: They've got a lot of *borrowing capacity* still.

segments.narration: Remember who often owns the building being remodelled.
Then there's you, the customer. In May 2024, an eighteen-dollar Big Mac meal went viral, and McDonald's had to respond.
McDonald's USA president Joe Erlinger wrote an open letter. That eighteen-dollar price, he said, came from one restaurant out of more than thirteen thousand seven hundred.

visual.label: Where the $18 Big Mac meal was found

segments.narration: He argued prices for many items had risen less than inflation, and that the viral claims of prices doubling were wrong.
He also pointed out that franchisees set their own menu prices, to cover rising wages, supply costs and inflation.

visual.text: Franchisees set prices to cover *historic rises* in supply chain costs, wages and other inflationary pressures.

segments.narration: But remember that survey. Owners say their control over prices has been weakened. So who is really deciding?
That's true. But it's also convenient. The company that collects a percentage of every sale isn't the one blamed for the price.
Customers noticed anyway. In July 2024, McDonald's global same-store sales fell one percent. The first drop since the pandemic.

visual.label: Global same-store sales
visual.sub: Q2 2024 · first drop since the pandemic

segments.narration: Kempczinski admitted that price increases had disrupted long-running value programs, and made people rethink their habits.

visual.text: These price increases disrupted long running value programs and led consumers to *reconsider* their buying habits.

segments.narration: He called lower-income customers the battleground.

visual.text: The battleground is with the *low-income* consumer.

segments.narration: So McDonald's launched a five-dollar meal deal that summer. In September 2025, it added Extra Value Meals, about fifteen percent cheaper than buying the items separately.
The limited-time offer was an eight-dollar Big Mac meal and a five-dollar Sausage McMuffin meal, a dollar more in California, Alaska, Hawaii and Guam.
Because lower-income customers were disappearing. McDonald's said their fast food visits fell by double-digit percentages across the industry.
Kempczinski said that absolutely is shaping value perceptions in a negative way.

visual.text: That absolutely is shaping *value perceptions* in a negative way.

segments.narration: And the five-dollar deal did help. McDonald's said that summer it was starting to bring visits back, after traffic had stayed soft through early 2024.
So, who made McDonald's so expensive?
The fair answer: a lot of it was real. Wages, food and paper all cost more, and franchisees set their own prices.
But look at the design. The franchisee takes the costs and the blame. The customer takes the price. And McDonald's takes a percentage, rent and royalty, off the top of every sale.
Look at the numbers again. Rent, ten point four billion. Royalties, six. Margin on the restaurants it runs itself, one point four.
My verdict: McDonald's isn't really selling you a burger. It's renting a building, and the burger pays the rent.
That model made Harry Sonneborn's idea one of the most successful in business history. And it explains why the company can thrive while owners and customers feel squeezed.
If you want to save money, use the app deals and value meals, and compare prices between locations. They really can differ.
And if this landlord trick sounds familiar, watch how airlines make more from your credit card than from flying. Same idea: the product you see isn't where the money is.
